text: Welcome to Chapter 5 — Flow in Practice. Nothing stops an org from building ten separate flows that all fire on the same object and event. This lesson is about why that's a real architecture problem, and the one pattern that fixes it.

Ten Before-Save flows on Case, built by ten different people over several years, each one solving its own narrow problem. Individually, every one looks reasonable. Together: nobody can predict the order they run in, debugging means opening ten flows instead of one, and eventually two of them quietly undo each other's work without anyone noticing.

Here's what that actually looks like in practice — five flows, each with its own narrow condition and its own update. Case Type equals Downtime, set Priority High. Case Origin equals Phone, assign to Phone Queue. Account Tier equals Platinum, set the SLA. Subject contains security, flag for review. Status equals Escalated, notify the manager. Five flows, five separate places this logic lives.

Salesforce's own recommendation is one flow per object per trigger context. Same five rules, but now they're Decision branches inside a single flow — one place to read, one place to debug, one predictable order of execution. The business logic didn't change at all. Where it lives did.

This isn't a one-time fix you apply to an existing mess. It's a check you run every time: before building flow number eleven, open the object's existing Before-Save or After-Save flow and ask whether this new rule is just another Decision branch in what's already there.

One flow per object per trigger context, with Decision elements doing the branching that used to be done by having separate flows decide independently whether to run. Next up: Naming Conventions and Documentation — because a single consolidated flow only stays readable if everything inside it is named like it matters.
